# The Whispering Airwaves: Resistance Radio in World War II

**Gallery 4 — Instruments of Defiance**

When Nazi forces occupied much of Europe after 1940, one of their first acts was to confiscate radios and make listening to foreign broadcasts—especially the BBC—a punishable offense, sometimes by death. Yet resistance networks understood that survival depended on communication. This exhibit displays the remarkable equipment they built and hid.

## Building the Sets

Resistance radio operators, often trained engineers or amateur "ham" radio enthusiasts, faced enormous obstacles. Commercial components were rationed, registered, or unavailable. So they improvised:

**Scavenged parts.** Valves (vacuum tubes) were the most precious components, pried from broken receivers, stolen from German depots, or smuggled from Allied airdrops. A single working tube could be worth more than a month's wages.

**Homemade coils and capacitors.** Operators wound coils around cardboard tubes, pill bottles, and wooden dowels. Capacitors were fashioned from waxed paper, foil, and even pages of books. Resistors might be lengths of pencil lead or carbon-coated string.

**Improvised power.** With mains electricity unreliable or dangerous to tap, sets ran on car batteries, flashlight cells, or hand-cranked generators. Some operators built rectifiers from stacks of copper and aluminum plates separated by cloth soaked in a borax solution.

**Concealment by design.** Radios were disguised as everyday objects—hidden inside bread loaves, hollowed-out books, suitcases with false bottoms, or beneath floorboards. Some sets were built small enough to fit in a coat pocket, with antennas strung along clotheslines or buried fences that doubled as ordinary wire.

## The Operator's World

Transmitting was deadly work. German direction-finding vans roamed cities triangulating illegal signals, so operators limited transmissions to minutes, changed frequencies constantly, and used ciphers to encode messages. The famous "numbers stations" and coded phrases broadcast by the BBC—*"Les sanglots longs des violons..."*—told agents across France that supplies were coming or missions were go.

## Remember

The objects in this case—scorched soldering irons, a valve hidden in a lipstick tube, a transmitter disguised as a cheese box—remind us that the resistance fought not only with courage, but with ingenuity, a soldering iron, and whatever the occupation economy left behind.

*On loan from the National Resistance Archive, with thanks to the families of the operators.*
